profile.reading: Hurricane Electric Fremont 2 sits at 48233 Warm Springs Boulevard, Fremont, California 94539. Hurricane Electric's own colocation page describes this as its largest facility, at 200,000 square feet with 3,000 cabinets, diverse A and B power with fully separate PDUs, panels, transformers, and generators, 13 internet exchange points including SFMIX and FCIX, 8 carriers with diverse fiber, and connections to 295 internet networks, alongside cabinet level surveillance, keycard access, onsite security, and 24 by 7 by 365 onsite staff and remote hands support. Hurricane Electric, per Wikipedia's own article, was established in 1994 by Mike Leber and operates under autonomous system number 6939, positioning itself as the largest global IP network by network adjacencies in both IPv4 and IPv6 as of June 2024, and the largest global IPv6 network by IPv6 prefixes announced. The company connects to more than 338 major exchange points, peers directly with more than 11,990 networks under an open peering policy requiring no contracts, and maintains more than 55 terabits per second of active public peering capacity and more than 900 terabits per second of private peering capacity. The company operates two other colocation facilities already on file elsewhere in this registry, a smaller sibling Fremont building known as Fremont 1, also the company's corporate headquarters address, and a San Jose facility at 55 South Market Street. Fremont sits in the southern San Francisco Bay Area, in Alameda County, a secondary but well established Bay Area colocation and interconnection market that offers lower real estate and power costs than downtown San Francisco or San Jose while remaining close enough to Silicon Valley's dense fiber infrastructure for network operators like Hurricane Electric to maintain the low latency peering relationships central to its business model.

reading.body:
Hurricane Electric's Fremont 2 facility holds 3,000 cabinets across 200,000 square feet, making it a major colocation hub in the Bay Area despite publishing no power consumption figures.

The facility is one of three that Hurricane Electric operates in Northern California. Hurricane Electric functions as both an internet service provider and network backbone operator, roles that typically require dense interconnection infrastructure. Colocation facilities like this one lease cabinet space to multiple tenants, which means power demand can vary widely depending on occupancy and customer workloads. The lack of published megawatt capacity makes it impossible to assess how much electricity this facility actually draws or how much headroom it has for AI workload growth.

The 200,000 square foot building with 3,000 cabinets suggests moderate density by data center standards. Without power figures, the data cannot establish whether this facility is a binding constraint on Bay Area compute availability or simply a regional node in a larger network. The facility's colocation model means it serves many operators rather than any single one, which shapes its role in the AI supply chain differently than a hyperscaler's owned-and-operated data center would.
